explainers.title: What the ESM actually is
explainers.lede: Your future employer is not a bank, not an EU institution, and not funded by taxes. Knowing exactly what it is explains almost every rule you will meet in the job.

p: The European Stability Mechanism (ESM) is the euro area's permanent crisis fund. It was created by a treaty between the countries that use the euro, signed on 2 February 2012, and it opened on 8 October 2012. Its job is to lend to a euro area country that can no longer borrow at a sustainable price on the financial markets.

It sits in Luxembourg City, on the Kirchberg plateau, and employs around 230 people from more than 50 nationalities. That is small. A commercial bank with a lending ceiling of 500 billion euro would have tens of thousands of staff. The ESM manages with a few hundred because it does a small number of very large transactions inside a very controlled process.

Between 2010 and 2012, several euro area governments could not sell their bonds at a reasonable interest rate. A bond is a promise to repay borrowed money on a fixed date. When investors stop buying a country's bonds, that country cannot pay salaries, pensions, or the debt falling due.

The first answer was the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), a temporary vehicle set up in 2010. The ESM replaced it as the permanent one. The EFSF still exists, but only to manage the loans it already made.

Between them, the EFSF and the ESM have paid out 295 billion euro to five countries: Ireland, Portugal, Greece, Spain and Cyprus. The last programme, for Greece, ended in August 2018. There has been no new one since, but the old loans still have to be serviced every day. That daily servicing is the work Project CASTOR is about.

blocks.h: Not an EU institution, and this matters
p: The European Commission, the European Parliament and the European Central Bank (ECB) are EU institutions. They were created by the EU treaties and act for the Union as a whole. The ESM is different. It is an intergovernmental organisation: created by its own separate treaty between the euro area states, owned by those states as shareholders, and governed by their finance ministers rather than by an EU procedure.

The consequences are practical. The ESM has its own staff rules, its own procurement rules and its own budget. When Project CASTOR runs a mini-competition under a framework contract, it does so under ESM rules, not under the EU procurement directives that bind a Commission department.

It also means the ESM works with EU institutions rather than inside them. The European Commission negotiates programme conditions on the ESM's behalf, in liaison with the ECB, while the ESM keeps the money, the risk and the legal relationship with the borrower.
Four numbers get confused constantly. Learn the difference once.

p: So where does a loan come from? The ESM borrows it. It issues bonds (debt maturing in more than a year) and bills (less than a year, currently three and six months) to investors such as pension funds, central banks and insurers, and lends the proceeds on.

The paid-in capital is not the loan money. It is the cushion that makes investors willing to lend to the ESM cheaply. Because 81 billion euro of real cash sits behind the promise, and 628 billion euro more can be called, the ESM borrows at rates close to the best sovereign borrowers and passes that low rate on. Its credit standing is worth more than its cash.
This is why ESM staff say no taxpayer money is used for the loans. About the lending, that is literally true: the cash comes from bond investors, and the borrower repays it with interest.

p: Voting weight follows each country's share of the capital, so Germany, France and Italy carry the largest weights. Three thresholds matter: mutual agreement, meaning unanimity among those voting, for the largest decisions including assistance; a qualified majority of 80% of votes cast for most others; and an emergency procedure at 85%, available when the Commission and the ECB both judge an urgent decision is needed to protect euro area stability.

blocks.h: What this means for Project CASTOR
p: Project CASTOR is not paid for out of the 500 billion euro. It comes from the administrative budget, the ESM's own running costs, which is a completely separate pot. Confusing the two is the most common beginner mistake in this field.

It also means CASTOR's approval route is entirely internal. In the story, the Corporate Investment Board decides which internal investments get funded, and Lorenzo de' Medici chairs it. The Board of Governors never hears the project's name. Keep the two governance worlds apart in your head: one governs money lent to countries, the other money spent on the institution itself.

explainers.title: The lending toolkit
explainers.lede: The ESM does not have one product. It has a shelf of them, and the whole point of Project CASTOR is that the new system must handle any of them without writing new code.

p: In lending, an instrument is a defined type of support with its own legal agreement, conditions, pricing and pattern of cash flows. Each behaves differently inside a system. A loan paid out in six tranches over three years is not the same object as a credit line that may never be drawn at all.
Here is the shelf. Read each one for what it is for, not for its name.

blocks.h: Loan under a macroeconomic adjustment programme
p: The classic rescue loan, and the biggest. It goes to a member state that has lost access to the markets. In exchange the country agrees a full reform programme covering its budget, its public sector and often its banks. The money is paid in tranches over years, and each tranche is released only after a review confirms the agreed measures were taken. Ireland, Portugal, Greece, Spain and Cyprus were all financed this way.

Here the problem is not the government but its banks. The ESM lends to the government, and the government puts the money into the banks. It is called indirect because the ESM's borrower is still the state, which stays liable for repayment. The conditions usually target financial supervision, bank governance and the national laws on restructuring and resolution. Spain's 2012 programme is the example.

The ESM injects capital into a bank itself instead of lending to the state, so that a failing bank does not drag its government's finances down with it. It is capped at 60 billion euro inside the 500 billion euro lending capacity, and it has never been used. It still matters for a system project: an instrument that has never been used must still be configured, tested and reportable.

Insurance, not treatment. A standby credit line for a country whose economy is fundamentally sound and which still has market access, but which could be hit by something outside its control. Eligibility is measured against published benchmarks: a government deficit below 3% of gross domestic product, debt below 60% of GDP or falling towards it, and no excessive imbalances. Instead of a Memorandum of Understanding the country signs a Letter of Intent, reviewed every six months. Credit lines of this kind are usually never drawn; their value is the signal.

The same idea for a country whose overall position is sound but which does not meet every PCCL benchmark. Because there is a known weakness, it signs a Memorandum of Understanding with specific corrective measures. Same shape of support, heavier conditions.

blocks.h: Primary and Secondary Market Support Facilities
p: The primary market is where a bond is first sold by its issuer. Under the Primary Market Support Facility the ESM buys newly issued bonds directly from a member state, normally alongside a programme, so that an auction does not fail and the country keeps a working link to investors.

The secondary market is where bonds are traded between investors after issue. Under the Secondary Market Support Facility the ESM buys existing bonds there to support liquidity when a disorderly market is itself the threat. It is the least used tool and the most politically sensitive, because it looks like intervening in prices.

A time-limited credit line created in May 2020 for the healthcare, cure and prevention costs of the Covid-19 crisis. No country drew on it and it expired at the end of 2022. Remember it as proof that the toolkit changes: a new instrument can be designed and approved in weeks when the politics allow, which puts the pressure onto whether the systems can follow.

blocks.h: The common backstop, which is planned and not live
p: The Single Resolution Fund (SRF) is the pot that pays for resolving failing banks in the Banking Union. It is filled by the banks themselves, not by governments, holds roughly 80 billion euro, and reached its target level of 1% of covered deposits at the end of 2023.

The 2021 reform of the ESM Treaty would add a credit line from the ESM to that fund, capped at 68 billion euro. If a resolution exhausted the SRF, the ESM would lend it the difference, repayable within three years and extendable to five, out of further bank contributions. Banks pay, not taxpayers.

Now the honest part. The amended Treaty was signed in January and February 2021 and enters into force only when every member state has ratified it. Italy has not, and as of 2026 it is the only one that has not. The backstop is designed, agreed and un-started. Anyone who tells you the ESM has a backstop today is wrong.

For Project CASTOR this is a requirement and a risk at once. The Business Case promises a new instrument can be switched on within six weeks of the Treaty entering into force, and nobody can say when that is. A system needing nine months of coding per instrument cannot make that promise. A system where an instrument is configuration can.

explainers.title: The life of a rescue loan
explainers.lede: This is what people mean by loan processing. Follow one euro from a government's request to its final repayment, and every job title in the building starts to explain itself.

p: A rescue loan is not one event. It is a chain of about fifteen controlled steps running over years. Different teams own different steps, and every hand-over between them is a place where money, or the record of money, can go wrong.
Two words first. A tranche is one instalment of an agreed loan. A disbursement is the act of paying one tranche out. A facility of 50 billion euro is never sent as one wire.

steps.d: A euro area government writes to the Chair of the Board of Governors asking for financial assistance. A political act with an exact legal form, usually after months of quiet discussion. What can go wrong: the request is delayed for domestic political reasons until the loan finally needed is larger.

The European Commission, in liaison with the European Central Bank and often the International Monetary Fund, assesses how much is needed, whether the debt can be repaid, and the risk to the euro area. The ESM runs its own analysis. What can go wrong: it rests on forecasts, and forecasts for a country in crisis are the least reliable that exist.

steps.t: 3. The programme and the Memorandum of Understanding
steps.d: The Commission negotiates a Memorandum of Understanding on the ESM's behalf: the reforms committed to, and the review timetable. This is where conditionality lives, because money arrives only when conditions are met. What can go wrong: conditions that look reasonable on paper prove politically impossible, and every review becomes a renegotiation.

The Board of Governors grants assistance by mutual agreement. The Board of Directors then approves the facility, and later each individual disbursement under it. What can go wrong: several member states need their national parliament to approve first, so the decision waits on a timetable nobody in Luxembourg controls.

The two sides sign a financial assistance facility agreement: amount, availability period, pricing, drawdown rules, events of default. Legal owns it, and from here everything is contractual. What can go wrong: a clause left slightly unclear becomes a dispute five years later, when everyone who negotiated it has moved on.

The ESM holds no pool of cash waiting to be lent. Treasury and Funding issue bonds and bills under a published plan, and the proceeds fund all loans from one shared pool. What can go wrong: a bad day on the bond market. The disbursement date is fixed by an agreement; the market is not.

Lending Operations creates the instruction: which facility, which tranche, how much, to which account, for which value date, against which approval. This is the object Project CASTOR revolves around. What can go wrong: a wrong account number, amount or date, or borrower bank details last verified two years ago.

A second, different person verifies the instruction against the underlying documents and approves it. Whoever created it may not release it. What can go wrong: the check degrades into a habit, or the system lets one person hold both roles. That second failure is an audit finding, and LOS had exactly that one.

The approved instruction becomes a formatted payment message and travels over a secure network to the banks that move the money, out of the ESM's own account at a central or correspondent bank. What can go wrong: it is rejected for a formatting error and must be repaired, eating the hours left before the cut-off.

Every payment system has a time of day after which an instruction can no longer settle for the value date you wanted. Miss it and the money arrives a day late. What can go wrong: a re-keying step starting at 15:40 for a 16:00 cut-off. This single mechanic is why SC1 exists.

On the value date the money must be in the receiving account and available. Value date is not the date the instruction was sent, nor the date it was booked. What can go wrong: one day late on 250 million euro costs real interest, and breaks the borrower's own payment plan for that day.

Somebody must prove that what the loan system says was paid, what the treasury system says was funded, and what the bank statement shows left the account are the same. Every unexplained difference is a break and must be cleared. What can go wrong: doing it three days later, by hand, in a spreadsheet. That was the LOS baseline, and SC2 attacks it.

From the value date the loan earns interest, building day by day. The system calculates it daily on the agreed rate basis and books it, whether or not cash moves. What can go wrong: a wrong day-count convention or a missed rate reset quietly mis-states the accounts for months.

The agreement fixes when interest and principal fall due. The system generates the forward cash flows, issues the notices, and posts each receipt against the right loan. What can go wrong: a rescheduling means regenerating the whole schedule without losing the record of what was true before.

The loan ends by running to its final maturity date, or because the country repays early, which several have done. Early repayment forces a recalculation of interest and can leave the ESM holding funding it no longer needs. What can go wrong: short notice, on a loan whose data has been migrated twice.

blocks.h: Where Project CASTOR sits in the chain
p: Steps 1 to 6 are political, legal and market work, and no IT project changes them. Steps 7 to 15 are operational, repetitive and measurable, which is exactly the stretch Project CASTOR automates. That is also why the five success criteria are shaped the way they are. Each one names a step.

p: When anyone says a payment is late, ask which step. Late because Board approval slipped is a governance problem. Late because the message was rejected is a data problem. Late because a person was re-keying at 15:40 is a process problem, and only the last one is something an IT project can fix.

The same discipline works in the PM2 exam. When a case study says a deliverable failed, the useful question is never whose fault it was, but which control should have caught it and whether that control existed.

explainers.title: Front, middle and back office
explainers.lede: Every financial institution splits one transaction between three teams that are deliberately not allowed to be the same people. Once you see the split, the organisation chart reads itself.

p: Front office, middle office and back office are not levels of seniority, and back office is not a polite word for junior. They are three stages of one transaction, separated on purpose.

rows: Faces the outside world and commits the institution. Negotiates, prices, agrees.
Lending Operations agreeing a facility and its drawdown schedule. Funding selling a bond to investors.

p: One rule sits underneath the whole design: the person who agrees a payment must not be the person who releases it. That rule is segregation of duties. Its everyday form is the four-eyes principle, where a second competent person checks and approves before anything takes effect.

This is not distrust of colleagues. It is a control built so an ordinary mistake gets caught, so a fraud would need two people instead of one, and, just as important, so the institution can prove afterwards that both were true. The proof is the audit trail: a stored record of who did what, when, and on what basis, which cannot be altered later.

In Project CASTOR this is not theory. Internal Audit raised two findings against LOS, one on segregation of duties and one on the completeness of the audit trail. Success criterion SC5 says both must be closed, and an audit finding closes only with evidence.

explainers.title: What a lending operations system is for
explainers.lede: Project CASTOR replaces a system called LOS. Until you know what a lending operations system does all day, the project is only a name and a budget.

p: A loan servicing system, also called a lending operations system, is the institutional memory of every loan plus the machine that acts on it. It holds what was agreed, works out what must happen next, makes it happen, and records that it happened. Everything else in the project is detail sitting on top of those four jobs.

blocks.h: The eight things it actually does

steps.d: It holds a definition of each instrument: how interest is calculated, which fees apply, how drawdowns work, what documents are required, what the accounting looks like. In a good system this is configuration, which a trained business user can change. In a bad system it is code, and every new instrument becomes a development project. That one difference is success criterion SC3: nine months down to six weeks.

The register of every facility and every loan: borrower, amount committed, amount drawn, amount outstanding, rate, dates, status. When someone asks what the exposure to a given country is, the loan book answers, and everything else is derived from it.

The agreed plan of when the borrower may take each tranche and on what conditions. The system does not merely record the plan, it enforces it: disbursing more than the facility allows, or earlier than the agreement permits, should be impossible.

From the loan terms the system calculates every future payment: interest dates, principal repayments, fees, and the daily accrual in between. This is the arithmetic engine. Change one rate reset and several hundred future amounts change with it, which is why it must never be a spreadsheet.

It turns a decision to pay into a structured instruction carrying every field the payment network needs, routes it for the four-eyes approval, and hands it to the payment gateway in the right format. This is the step that must be automatic, because it is currently done three times by hand.

Every event, whether a disbursement, an accrual, a receipt or a fee, must produce matching double-entry bookkeeping in the general ledger. If the loan system and the ledger disagree, the month-end close stops until somebody finds the difference.

The system compares its own record against the bank statements and the treasury system, matches everything that matches, and puts the rest into an exception queue for a person. The goal is not zero exceptions, but that a human only ever sees a genuine one.

Management reports, accounting reports, regulatory reporting to supervisors on a fixed timetable, and the ad hoc question a Board member asks on a Tuesday. All built from the same data, so that all of them agree with each other.

p: Straight-through processing, usually written STP, means a transaction passes from one system to the next automatically, from end to end, with nobody retyping anything on the way.

Notice what it does not mean. A human still decides, and a human still approves. STP does not remove the four-eyes check, and any vendor who says it does should worry you. It removes the keyboard between the systems, not the judgement between the people.

In LOS today, a disbursement instruction is typed into the loan system, then typed again into the treasury system, then typed again into the payment gateway. That is manual re-keying, and roughly 1,400 fields a quarter go through it. Success criterion SC4 sets the target at zero, which is a strong word chosen deliberately: 90% automated still means a person is retyping under time pressure on the hardest cases.

blocks.h: Why re-keying is worse than it looks
p: It is slow. Every re-keying step needs a specific person to be available and free at exactly the moment before a cut-off. That is what puts a floor under the five working day cycle time SC1 attacks. You cannot compress a queue of humans.

It fails silently. A transcription error does not make the system complain. A wrong digit produces a perfectly valid, perfectly wrong payment, and because the two records now disagree, it surfaces days later as a reconciliation break at the worst possible moment.

And it is an audit finding. An auditor does not ask whether you got it right. An auditor asks whether you can prove only authorised people did this, and then asks to see the record. A re-keyed field breaks the chain of evidence, because the value in the second system has no verified link to the value in the first. That is why closing the LOS findings is a success criterion rather than a nice-to-have.

blocks.h: So what is Project CASTOR, in one paragraph
p: It replaces a 14-year-old system, built in the EFSF era, in which each instrument is hard-coded, instructions are re-keyed three times, reconciliation takes three working days, and the audit trail has holes in it. It buys and configures a platform where an instrument is a set of settings, the chain from loan agreement to disbursement to repayment schedule runs automatically, reconciliation completes the same day, every action is logged, and a new instrument such as the common backstop could be switched on within six weeks of the Treaty reform entering into force.

The price of that is 8.4 million euro, 3,100 person-days and 26 months, delivered as a mix: an in-house core team plus an outsourced platform implementation by Levallois Systems. Every argument in the story is downstream of those three sentences.

explainers.title: Why replacing a working system is hard
explainers.lede: Replacing a system that works is harder than building one that does not exist yet, and nearly every crisis in the CASTOR story comes from one of six causes.

p: A new system in an empty space has no history, no users, no live money and no deadline belonging to somebody else. A replacement has all four. The old system keeps paying, keeps accruing, keeps being audited and keeps being changed while you build the thing that will switch it off.

A parallel run means both systems process the same real work at the same time and you compare the results. It is the only honest proof that the new system is right, because it tests against reality instead of against your expectations of reality.

It is also expensive in the one resource you cannot buy: for the whole period, the business does its job twice. CASTOR runs parallel from 08 Jan to 30 Apr 2028, chosen so the window covers a month-end close and a quarter-end.

What breaks it is a real event the two systems handle differently. In the story an EFSF bond rollover lands in the middle of the run, the reconciliation report does not match, and Marie Curie refuses acceptance. That is the process working, not failing.
Every loan, every schedule, every historical cash flow and every document reference has to move from the old system into the new one without changing. Without changing is the hard part.

Old systems accumulate records that break their own rules: a loan with no end date, an amount stored as text, a counterparty renamed in 2014 and never merged, a fee type only three loans use and nobody can explain. You cannot migrate what you cannot explain, and you cannot explain it quickly.
Migration is normally the largest single underestimate in this kind of project, and it is found late, because everybody tests the clean 97% and nobody looks at the ugly 3% until the rehearsal.

Cutover is the moment you switch the old system off and the new one on. In a financial institution the project does not choose the window; the payment calendar chooses it. It must fall between value dates, outside the month-end close, away from an interest payment date and away from a bond maturity. CASTOR goes live on 15 May 2028, which looks arbitrary until you notice it sits after the April month-end and well before the June quarter-end.

Every cutover also needs a rollback plan: the agreed way of returning to the old system if the switch fails. A rollback plan is not real unless three things are written down before the weekend starts. A decision point, a named person allowed to call it, and the last moment at which calling it is still possible.

A regression is something that used to work and now does not. A regression pack is a fixed set of tests re-run after every change, to prove nothing which worked has broken. On a lending system the pack is large, because the arithmetic multiplies out: instrument type times rate basis times day-count convention times fee structure times repayment pattern. Each combination can be quietly wrong.

Teams under time pressure shrink the pack, usually by dropping combinations that have never failed. That is the most reliable method known for producing a live incident, and it is exactly what an independent Project Quality Assurance reviewer is there to notice.

In every specialist system, one or two people carry knowledge that exists nowhere else. That is a risk before they leave and an issue on the day they do. CASTOR names it as risk R-07 against Nikola Tesla, the lead architect seconded from Levallois Systems. On 04 Oct 2027 he resigns, and the entry moves from the Risk Log to the Issue Log. That move is the whole distinction PM2 draws between a risk, which might happen, and an issue, which has happened.

The defences are all boring and all have to exist before the day: a key-person clause in the contract, design decisions written down rather than remembered, a named deputy, and knowledge transfer with real time reserved for it. Every one is cheap in advance and impossible to arrange afterwards.

blocks.h: 6. Why you cannot have a change freeze
p: In most replacement projects the business agrees a change freeze: no new features on the old system while the new one is built. A financial-assistance institution cannot promise that. If a member state requests support, or the Treaty reform enters into force, or a supervisor changes a reporting requirement, the change is not optional and its date is not negotiable. So CASTOR must plan for changes it cannot predict, arriving at moments it cannot control, landing on both systems at once.

This is why the paperwork matters more here than elsewhere. The pressure to say yes informally is constant. In the story a verbal request arrives from a Board member's cabinet asking for backstop screens now. Handled as a favour it destroys the baseline quietly. Handled properly it becomes a Change Request Form, an entry in the Change Log and a Project Steering Committee decision, and then the answer, whatever it is, is defensible.
