The interest a bond pays its holders, and the rate that defines it.
A 3 billion euro bond with a 3% annual coupon costs its issuer 90 million euro a year, on a date fixed years in advance.
Repaying debt that is falling due by issuing new debt, usually on the same day.
An EFSF bond matures and a new one is issued to repay it. Large cash flows move in both directions on one date, which is why a rollover in the middle of a parallel run is dangerous.
Repaying a loan gradually in instalments, instead of all at the end.
A loan amortising over ten years repays about 10% of the principal each year. A bullet loan repays 100% on the final day and nothing before it.
The headline amount a contract is written on, used to calculate payments. It is not necessarily an amount that moves.
A 50 billion euro facility has a 50 billion euro notional even if only 30 billion euro has ever been drawn.
Assets pledged to the lender, which the lender may take if the borrower does not pay.
ESM loans to states are not collateralised. Treasury investments and derivative contracts are, and the collateral is revalued daily.
Revaluing something at what it is worth in the market today, instead of what was paid for it.
The invested paid-in capital is marked to market, so its reported value moves up and down as interest rates move.

p: First, always ask which date somebody means. Trade date, booking date, value date and settlement date are four different things, and in any payment discussion at least two of them are in the room without being named. The instruction says one, the accounts say another, and the difference is usually the whole argument.

Second, always ask basis points of what, and over what period. A margin is quoted in basis points on the amount outstanding, per year. A fee may be a one-off percentage of the entire facility. The ESM's own service fee, for example, has an upfront component of 50 basis points plus a small annual component of half a basis point. Same unit, completely different amounts of money.

blocks.h: Three more you will meet almost as often
p: Day-count convention. Interest quoted per year has to be turned into interest for a particular 31 days, and there is more than one rule for doing that: actual/360, actual/365, 30/360. The choice is written in the loan agreement and it changes the number. It is also a classic cause of a reconciliation break between two systems that were configured by two different people in two different years.

Principal and interest. Principal is the borrowed amount itself. Interest is the price paid for having it. A repayment is usually a mixture, and the split matters, because they are accounted for differently and reported differently. When a schedule looks wrong, check the split first.

Face value against market value. Face value, also called nominal or par, is the amount printed on the debt and repaid at maturity. Market value is what somebody would pay for it today. A bond issued at 100 and trading at 97 has not changed what it will repay. It has changed what it is worth to hold. Confusing the two is how people misread a balance sheet.

Do not try to memorise the list. Take one word into the next conversation you have and use it correctly once. Terminology sticks through use, not through revision, and in this industry using a word correctly is how people decide whether to explain the next thing to you or not.

explainers.title: Reading Project CASTOR's numbers
explainers.lede: Three numbers describe the shape of any project: money, effort and time. Divide them into each other and the project tells you what it really is.

p: Project CASTOR is 8.4 million euro, 3,100 person-days and 26 months, running from a Project Initiation Request on 12 Jan 2026 to administrative closure on 28 Jul 2028. On their own, none of those numbers means anything. Divided into each other, they describe a specific kind of project, and they let you say straight away whether a plan is plausible.

rows: Too high to be all labour. So part of the 8.4 million euro is not people: platform licences, infrastructure, and fixed-price elements of the contractor's work.
Roughly five to six people working full time, averaged across the project. A small, senior team, not an army.
Long enough that people will leave, the budget year rolls over twice, and the institutional context moves underneath the project.
3,100 person-days across two releases and a parallel run
Expect a light Initiating and Planning period, a heavy Executing period, and a second peak at parallel run and cutover in 2028.

p: A person-day, written PD, is one person working for one day. It is the unit PM2 uses for effort, and it is deliberately separate from duration. One hundred person-days can be one person for a hundred days or ten people for ten days, and those are completely different projects with completely different risks. The other unit you will meet is the full-time equivalent, or FTE, which is one person working full time for a year.

blocks.h: The five success criteria, read properly

rows: Disbursement cycle time, instruction to value date
Speed. It is the only criterion the borrowing country would notice directly.
Control. A three-day gap is three days in which an error is live and nobody knows.
Flexibility. It is the only criterion about the future rather than about today, and the only one nobody can test until a new instrument arrives.
about 1,400 fields per quarter to zero
Effort and risk at once. Every field is a chance to be wrong and a person who has to be available.
Compliance. Binary, judged by somebody outside the project, and impossible to argue down.

p: Notice what all five have in common. Each one has a baseline, a target and a unit. That is what makes a criterion measurable instead of an aspiration. Improve efficiency is not a success criterion. Reconciliation completed the same day, from a baseline of three working days, is.

This is worth carrying into the exam. A Business Case that states benefits without stating a baseline is incomplete, because you can never afterwards prove you delivered them. When a case study gives you a vague objective, the correct instinct is to ask what it is being measured against today.

blocks.h: Why the benefits only appear in 2029
p: Go-live is 15 May 2028, the Ready for Closing gate is 22 Jun 2028, and administrative closure completes on 28 Jul 2028. So on the day the project ends, the new system has been live for about ten weeks.

Ten weeks is not enough to measure any of SC1 to SC5 honestly. Reconciliation performance has to be seen across quarter-ends and a year-end close. Disbursement cycle time needs enough real disbursements to be more than an anecdote. Instrument onboarding cannot be measured at all until a new instrument arrives, which depends on a ratification nobody controls. The first full year of live running is 2029.

This is not a flaw in CASTOR. It is normal for every system replacement, and PM2 handles it explicitly. The project closes, and the Project-End Report hands benefit tracking to the permanent organisation: the standing departments that carry on after the project team is dissolved. The Project Owner does not stop being accountable for the benefits. She stops being accountable for a project.

Florence Nightingale finds this genuinely hard, and the reason is characterisation rather than accounting. She is the person who counts things. Being told the number she cares about will exist eighteen months after her project is archived is, for her, the most uncomfortable moment in the method.

blocks.h: How to read any project this way

steps.t: Divide the money by the effort
steps.d: If the cost per person-day is far above a plausible daily rate, the budget contains things that are not people. Find them, and ask for each whether it is an estimate or a quotation. Estimates move; quotations mostly do not.

steps.t: Divide the effort by the duration
steps.d: That gives you the average team size. If it is unrealistically small for the scope described, the plan is optimistic. If it is very large, the cost of coordinating everybody will eat part of the estimate.

steps.t: Ask when the benefit can first be measured
steps.d: If the honest answer is after the project closes, the Business Case needs a named owner for benefit tracking after closure. It also means the project's own success cannot be judged by the benefits, only by whether it delivered the capability to produce them.

steps.t: Check that every criterion has a baseline
steps.d: No baseline means no proof. This is the fastest weakness to spot in any Business Case, and it is a reliable source of marks in a PM2 exam question that asks what is missing.

steps.t: Look at where the dates sit in the business calendar
steps.d: A go-live date, a parallel run window or a cutover weekend that ignores month-end, quarter-end or a payment calendar is a plan written by somebody who has not asked the business. In CASTOR, every 2028 date has been chosen around that calendar.

glossary.d: The full set of conditions a deliverable must meet before the client will accept it, agreed before the work starts rather than argued afterwards.
One single measurable condition from that set. Measurable is the operative word: pass or fail must not be a matter of opinion.
The check that proves a requirement has really been met. It is agreed before the work starts, not invented when the work is delivered.
The supplier's commercial manager for a client. He owns the revenue and the relationship, not the delivery, and that difference matters when a project is in trouble.
An amount earned or owed but not yet paid, recognised a little at a time as the days pass rather than all at once when cash moves.
A one-off report written to answer a specific need the regular reports do not cover. Each one costs effort that was not planned.
The ESM's own running costs: salaries, buildings, systems and projects. It is a completely separate pot of money from the lending capacity.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR's 8.4 million euro comes from here.

glossary.d: Repaying a loan gradually in instalments instead of all at the end. A loan amortising over ten years repays about a tenth of the principal each year.
The senior committee, written AGB, that approves a project, agrees its objectives and releases its money. It sits above the project, not inside it.
glossary.more: In Project CASTOR it is the Corporate Investment Board, chaired by Lorenzo de' Medici.

glossary.d: The in-house advisers, written AO, on how the organisation's IT systems should fit together. They ask what problem is being solved before discussing a solution.
glossary.more: Albert Einstein represents them on the Project Steering Committee.

glossary.d: A sale in which investors bid for a new issue of debt and the issuer accepts the best bids. A failed auction is one where too few bids arrive.
The stored record of who changed what, when, and on what basis, kept so that it cannot be altered afterwards.
glossary.more: One of the two internal-audit findings against LOS was that its audit trail was incomplete.

glossary.d: The total value of the shares the ESM's members have subscribed to, about 709 billion euro. Most of it has never been paid in.
The window during which a borrower may still draw money under a facility. When it closes, anything not drawn is cancelled.
The formal decision giving a contract to one supplier after a competition, and the point from which the contract governs everything.
glossary.more: Contract award to Levallois Systems: 18 Sep 2026.

glossary.d: The team that settles, confirms, pays, books and reconciles after a deal has been agreed. It produces the accounting record.
Funding a loan with borrowing whose cash flows match it exactly, date for date. Used for particular purposes rather than as the normal method.
The shared European system for supervising banks and dealing with failing ones, covering the euro area and any other member state that joins it.
The ESM's own average cost of funding, calculated daily across all the bonds and bills it has issued. Loan pricing is built on top of it.
The approved version of scope, cost and dates that progress is measured against. Changing it needs the change process, not a decision in a corridor.
The agreed and approved set of requirements. From the moment it is baselined, adding anything requires a change request.
One hundredth of one percent. One hundred basis points make 1%. Written bp and spoken as bip.
glossary.more: A margin of 25 basis points on 250 million euro is 625,000 euro a year.

glossary.d: Actually obtaining the improvements a project promised. It usually happens after the project has closed, which is normal rather than a failure.
A short-term tradable debt security maturing in less than a year. The ESM currently issues bills at three and six months.

One director and one alternate per euro area member state, appointed for their competence in economic and financial matters. It exercises the powers the governors delegate, including approving each disbursement.
The ESM's highest decision-making body: one governor per member state, in practice the finance minister. It decides whether to grant financial assistance at all.
A tradable promise to repay borrowed money on a fixed future date, usually paying interest along the way. Debt maturing in more than one year.
glossary.more: The ESM raises the money it lends by issuing bonds to investors.

glossary.d: A rollover done with bonds specifically: a maturing bond is repaid out of the proceeds of a new one issued for the purpose.
glossary.more: In the story an EFSF bond rollover lands in the middle of the parallel run and breaks the reconciliation report.

glossary.d: Repaying the whole principal in one payment on the final day, with only interest paid before that.
How fast a project is consuming its person-days or its money. Compared against progress, it is an early warning that an estimate was wrong.
A Project Core Team member who turns a business need into a specification the builders can work from. It is a job, not a PM2 role of its own.
glossary.more: Ada Lovelace, translating Grace Hopper's need into something Nikola Tesla can build.

glossary.d: The document that states the problem, compares options, justifies the money and recommends one solution, with measurable success criteria.
glossary.more: Approved with the Project Charter on 24 Mar 2026.

glossary.d: The written plan for keeping the work going when a critical system or building is unavailable, including who decides to invoke it.
The business and user staff, written BIG, who prepare their own teams for the coming change. They are worried about their own workload, and they are right to be.
The plan for changing processes, people, structures and culture so that the new system is actually used and the benefits actually arrive.
glossary.more: It moves the people. The Transition Plan moves the work.

glossary.d: The Project Owner's representative on the business side, written BM. Runs the day-to-day business involvement and keeps the business ready for the change.
glossary.more: Grace Hopper. She coordinates the Business Implementation Group.

glossary.d: The small private office of a senior official or board member. Its staff speak with that person's authority, which is why a request from a cabinet feels like an instruction.
glossary.more: In the story a cabinet asks verbally for backstop screens. It still has to become a Change Request Form.

glossary.d: The part of the subscribed capital that has not been paid, about 628 billion euro. It is a binding promise that members will pay if the ESM ever calls it.
A formal demand by the ESM that its members pay in part of their callable capital, under rules fixed in the ESM Treaty.
The markets where organisations raise money by selling bonds and shares to investors, rather than by borrowing from a bank.
The system's calculation of every future payment on a loan: interest dates, principal repayments, fees and the daily accrual in between.
The public institution that issues a currency and runs the payment system for it. In the euro area, the European Central Bank with the national central banks.
The register of requested changes, their assessment, and the decision taken on each one. It is what makes scope creep visible.
A formal written request to change something that has already been approved and baselined.
The form that turns a spoken request into an assessed, decided and recorded change, with an impact on scope, time, cost and quality.
glossary.more: The story's test case: a verbal request from a Board member's cabinet must become one of these.

glossary.d: A company that places itself between the buyer and the seller of a trade and guarantees to both that it will settle, taking the risk that one of them fails.
Assets pledged to a lender, which the lender may take and sell if the borrower does not pay.
glossary.more: ESM loans to states are not collateralised. Treasury investments and derivative contracts are.

glossary.d: A fee charged on money that has been promised but not yet drawn, to cover the lender's cost of keeping it available.
A planned ESM credit line to the Single Resolution Fund, capped at 68 billion euro, to be repaid by bank contributions. It needs the 2021 ESM Treaty reform ratified first.
glossary.more: Italy has not ratified, so the backstop is designed and agreed but not live.

glossary.d: The principle that assistance money is released only when the agreed conditions have actually been met, checked review by review.
The three properties information security protects: only the right people can see data, the data is correct and unaltered, and it is there when needed.
glossary.more: The remit of the Local Information Security Officer, Alan Turing in the story.

glossary.d: Controlling versions and access so that you can prove afterwards which version of a document or system was actually used, and by whom.
A situation where someone's private interest could affect a decision they help to take. It must be declared, and usually means standing aside.
The contractor's own periodic report to the client's Project Manager, on a schedule and in a format fixed by the contract.
The supplier's own project manager, usually written CPM. Reports to the client's Project Manager and, if necessary, to the Project Steering Committee.
glossary.more: Gustave Eiffel in the story. Courteous, contractual and immovable.

glossary.d: The correction or penalty the contract allows the client to demand when a supplier fails to deliver. It only exists if somebody wrote it in.
The table setting each member state's share of ESM capital, based mainly on the size of its economy and population. It also fixes voting weight.
glossary.more: Germany holds about 26.7%, France about 20.1%, Italy about 17.6%.

glossary.d: A team regularly checking its own controls and reporting the result, rather than waiting for an auditor to check them.
In Project CASTOR, the internal committee that decides which investments the institution funds and reviews the whole portfolio. It is the project's Appropriate Governance Body.
glossary.more: Chaired in the story by Lorenzo de' Medici. A fictional body, used to teach the AGB role.

glossary.d: A bank that holds an account for another institution and makes and receives payments on its behalf, usually in a market where it has no branch of its own.
The account a project charges its costs to. When it is closed at administrative closure, nothing further can be charged to the project.
glossary.more: Closing it is one of the last acts of Project CASTOR, on 28 Jul 2028.

glossary.d: Earned value divided by actual cost, written CPI. Below 1 means each euro is buying less than a euro of finished work.
The other party to a transaction. For an ESM loan it is the borrowing member state; for a treasury deal it is the bank on the other side.
The interest a bond pays its holders, and the rate that defines it. A 3 billion euro bond with a 3% coupon costs its issuer 90 million euro a year.
Bank deposits protected by a deposit guarantee scheme, in the European Union up to 100,000 euro per depositor per bank. The Single Resolution Fund's target size is 1% of them.
An agency's published opinion of how likely a borrower is to repay. A high rating lowers the interest rate the borrower must pay.
glossary.more: The ESM's own rating is why it can borrow cheaply and lend on cheaply.

glossary.d: The longest chain of dependent tasks through a project. Any delay on it delays the whole project, because there is no slack anywhere in the chain.
A condition that must hold or the project cannot succeed, no matter what else goes well. Not the same as a success criterion.
The moment the old system is switched off and the new one switched on. In a financial institution the payment calendar chooses the date, not the project.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR goes live on 15 May 2028, after the April close and before the June quarter-end.

glossary.d: Moving records from an old system into a new one without losing or changing anything. The hard part is the small share of records that break their own rules.
glossary.more: Usually the largest single underestimate in a system replacement.

glossary.d: The person, written DPC, who advises a project on the rules for handling personal data and on how to follow them.
glossary.more: Louis Brandeis, who co-wrote the article that invented privacy law.

glossary.d: The rule for turning a yearly interest rate into interest for a particular number of days, such as actual/360 or 30/360. It is written into the loan agreement.
glossary.more: A classic cause of a reconciliation break when two systems are configured differently.

glossary.d: The register of decisions taken on a project, with who took them, when, and on what basis.
Shutting a system down for good, once its data and its duties have moved somewhere else. It costs real money and is regularly forgotten in the Business Case.
glossary.more: LOS is decommissioned after the CASTOR parallel run ends.

glossary.d: Failing to meet an obligation in a loan or bond, most obviously by not paying on time.
Something the project hands over: a piece of software, a report, a migrated data set, or trained staff.
The signed record that a deliverable met its criteria and has been accepted, with any open points listed and dated.
A link that stops one task from starting until another one finishes. Dependencies, not effort, are what make a schedule long.
The person or body that decides how the system is built and who may change that design. Without one, every developer's opinion is equally valid.
An ESM instrument allowing capital to be put into a bank directly instead of lending to its government. Capped at 60 billion euro and never used.
glossary.more: Never used still means it must be configured, tested and reportable in the new system.

glossary.d: Paying out an agreed part of a loan to the borrower on a fixed date. One loan is normally paid in several disbursements over years, not all at once.
glossary.more: The disbursement instruction is the object Project CASTOR is built around.

glossary.d: The structured order to pay one tranche: which facility, how much, to which account, for which value date, against which approval. A second person must approve it before it is released.
glossary.more: In the story it is the document Marie Curie is working on in the opening scene.

glossary.d: Raising money through a mix of instruments and maturities and lending it from one shared pool, rather than matching each loan to its own borrowing.
The person, written DMO, responsible for versions, copies, retention and safe disposal of a project's documents.
The rule that every accounting entry is recorded twice, as a debit in one account and an equal credit in another, so the books always balance.
The agreed plan of when a borrower may take each tranche of a loan, and under what conditions. A good lending system enforces the plan, it does not merely record it.
A full rehearsal of a process on real data, with none of the results going live. It is how you find out that step 14 takes two hours, not twenty minutes.
A borrower repaying before the agreed date. It forces a recalculation of interest and can leave the lender holding funding it no longer needs.
glossary.more: Several former programme countries have repaid ESM or EFSF loans early.

glossary.d: The budgeted cost of the work actually finished, used to compare real progress against real spending instead of against opinion.
Enhanced Conditions Credit Line: standby support for a country that is broadly sound but does not meet every PCCL benchmark, so it signs a memorandum of understanding with corrective measures.
European Financial Stability Facility: the temporary euro area rescue fund set up in 2010, which the ESM replaced. It still manages its old loans but makes no new ones.
glossary.more: The system Project CASTOR replaces was built in the EFSF era, which is why it is 14 years old.

glossary.d: A faster ESM decision route at 85% of votes cast, available when the European Commission and the European Central Bank both judge an urgent decision is needed to protect euro area stability.
The agreed route for pushing a decision up to a higher level: who decides what, at which level, and how quickly.
Something valuable left with a neutral third party and released only on an agreed trigger. For software it is the source code, released if the supplier fails or goes out of business.
European Stability Mechanism: the euro area's permanent crisis fund. An intergovernmental organisation based in Luxembourg that lends to member states which have lost access to the markets.
glossary.more: Around 230 staff from more than 50 nationalities. Project CASTOR is a fictional ESM project.

glossary.d: The treaty between the euro area states that created the ESM, signed on 2 February 2012. A 2021 amendment adding new tasks has not yet entered into force.
The group of European Union member states that use the euro as their currency. Bulgaria became the twenty-first on 1 January 2026.
The informal meeting of euro area finance ministers. Its President chairs the ESM Board of Governors by convention.
The central bank of the euro area, usually written ECB. It advises on ESM assessments and attends ESM board meetings as an observer.
The European Union's executive body. It negotiates and signs programme conditions on the ESM's behalf, in liaison with the European Central Bank.
A situation listed in a loan agreement that allows the lender to demand immediate repayment, such as a missed payment or a false statement by the borrower.
Dealing with the cases a system cannot process automatically. Good design aims for few exceptions, each one genuinely needing a human decision.
The list of records the system could not match or process by itself, waiting for a person to work through them.
How much a lender or investor stands to lose if one particular counterparty fails to pay. It is the amount at risk, not the amount agreed.
The amount printed on a debt security, which is what will be repaid at maturity. Also called nominal or par value. It is not what the security is worth today.
The total amount a lender has agreed to make available, and the agreement that governs it. Money is drawn from a facility in tranches.
The rule that a second competent person must check and approve work before it takes effect. The everyday form of segregation of duties.
glossary.more: Straight-through processing removes the retyping, never the four-eyes check.

glossary.d: A contract agreed in advance with one or more suppliers, setting terms under which later individual orders can be placed quickly.
glossary.more: Levallois Systems is awarded the CASTOR work under an existing framework contract.

glossary.d: The unit that faces the outside world and commits the institution. It negotiates, prices and agrees deals.
One person working full time for a year, written FTE. A way of counting staff effort when people are shared between jobs.
The central accounting record of an institution, where every transaction is booked. If the loan system and the ledger disagree, the books cannot be closed.
How much damage a risk would do if it happened, scored from 1 to 5 against the project's objectives.
An ESM loan to a government which the government then puts into its own banks. The state stays liable for repayment. Spain's 2012 programme worked this way.
A defined type of financial support with its own legal agreement, conditions, pricing and pattern of cash flows. Each one behaves differently inside a system.
glossary.more: The ESM has about nine, which is why the new platform must be instrument-agnostic.

glossary.d: Interest building up on a loan day by day, recognised in the accounts before any cash is actually paid or received.
The document that says exactly what data two systems exchange, in what format, how often, and what happens when a message fails.
A body created by a treaty between states rather than by the European Union's own treaties. It has its own rules, budget and staff regulations.
glossary.more: This is why the ESM is not an EU institution and does not follow EU procurement directives.

glossary.d: A written weakness raised by the institution's own auditors. It is closed only with evidence that the weakness has actually been fixed.
glossary.more: Two open findings on LOS. Closing both is success criterion SC5.

glossary.d: A global institution, usually written IMF, that lends to countries in balance-of-payments trouble. It took part in several euro area programmes alongside the ESM and the EFSF.
The act of creating and selling new bonds or bills to raise money. The organisation doing it is the issuer.
An unplanned event that has already happened and needs a management action. A risk might happen; an issue has happened.
The register of things that have already gone wrong and need action now, with owner, size, priority and status.
glossary.more: Risk R-07 moves from the Risk Log to the Issue Log the day Tesla resigns.

glossary.d: A contract term obliging the supplier to replace a named expert with someone equivalent, and to hand over their work properly.
glossary.more: The defence against key-person risk. Useless unless agreed before the person resigns.

glossary.d: The danger that one person leaves and takes with them knowledge that exists nowhere else.
glossary.more: Risk R-07 in Project CASTOR, against the architect Nikola Tesla. It becomes an issue when he resigns.

glossary.d: Planned time in which one expert deliberately teaches others what only they know, with the result written down.
glossary.more: The only defence against key-person risk that works after the person has gone.

glossary.d: An old system that still works and still matters, which is why replacing it is harder than building something new.
glossary.more: LOS is 14 years old and was built for the EFSF era.

glossary.d: The ceiling in the ESM Treaty on how much may be lent to member states at one time: 500 billion euro, of which roughly 433 billion euro is still free.
glossary.more: It never pays for staff, buildings or projects. Those come from the administrative budget.

glossary.d: Written notes on what worked and what did not, kept so the next project does not repeat the same mistakes.
The running list a project keeps while it is still going. Waiting until the end means you only remember the last month.
The lighter alternative to a memorandum of understanding, used for a Precautionary Conditioned Credit Line. The country sets out its policy commitments and is reviewed every six months.
How probable it is that a risk actually happens, scored from 1, very low, to 5, very high.
How easily something can be turned into cash without moving its price. Also used for having enough cash available to meet obligations when they fall due.
The contract between lender and borrower fixing the amount, the price, the dates, the drawdown rules and what counts as default. At the ESM it is called a financial assistance facility agreement.
The register of every facility and loan an institution holds: borrower, amount committed, amount drawn, amount outstanding, rate, dates and status.
glossary.more: When somebody asks what our exposure to a country is, the loan book answers.

glossary.d: The system that holds every loan's terms, works out what must happen next, produces the instructions and records the result.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR replaces one of these, called LOS, built in the EFSF era.

glossary.d: The person, written LISO, responsible for the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the information a project handles.
The full package of budget and reform measures a country agrees to carry out in exchange for a rescue loan, with money released only as reviews are passed.
A difference big enough to change what the Business Case or the Project Charter approved. It goes above the Project Steering Committee.
The head of the ESM, appointed by the Board of Governors for a renewable five-year term. Chairs the Board of Directors and runs the institution day to day.
glossary.more: The story's equivalent is fictional. No real post-holder is portrayed.

glossary.d: Typing the same data into a second system by hand. It is slow, it fails silently, and it breaks the chain of evidence an auditor needs.
glossary.more: Success criterion SC4 targets zero, from a baseline of about 1,400 fields a quarter.

glossary.d: A charge added on top of the lender's own cost of funding, expressed in basis points per year, reflecting the risk of that particular loan or instrument.
Revaluing something at what it is worth in the market today, instead of at the price originally paid.
glossary.more: The ESM's invested paid-in capital is marked to market, so its reported value moves with interest rates.

glossary.d: A borrower's ability to raise money from investors at a price it can afford. Losing it is what turns a fiscal problem into a crisis.
glossary.more: Losing market access is the condition that makes a country eligible for an ESM programme loan.

glossary.d: What something would fetch if sold today, as opposed to what was paid for it or what it will repay at maturity.
The date on which a loan or bond must be fully repaid. Also used for the length of time remaining until that date.
The list of points, times and owners circulated before a meeting. Without it, the loudest topic wins.
The document, usually written MoU, listing the policy conditions a country commits to in exchange for assistance. The European Commission negotiates and signs it on the ESM's behalf.
The unit that independently checks, values and controls what the front office agreed, and owns the limits and the analysis.
A dated point in a plan marking that something significant has been completed. A milestone has no duration and no effort of its own.
A short competition held only between the suppliers already on a framework contract, to decide which of them gets a specific order.
The short official record of a meeting: what was raised, what was decided, and who does what by when.
The accounting work of finishing, checking and locking one month's figures. System changes are kept away from it because it cannot be paused.
glossary.more: It is why the CASTOR cutover date, 15 May 2028, sits after the April close.

glossary.d: A way of ranking requirements as Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time. The last category is the one that does the work.
Unanimity among the members who take part in a vote. Most large ESM decisions, including granting financial assistance, need it.
The overnight run that moves and processes a day's records between systems. If it fails, the working day starts with yesterday's problem.
A place where the work does not match the agreed standard, rule or specification. It is a statement about the work, not about the person.
Our account, held at another bank or at a central bank, out of which the institution actually pays and into which it receives.
glossary.more: The statement of the nostro account is the document reconciliation is checked against.

glossary.d: The time an employee or contractor must keep working after resigning, fixed in their contract. It is the window in which knowledge transfer is still possible.
The headline amount a contract is written on, used to calculate payments. It is not necessarily an amount of money that ever moves.
A purchase competition open to any company that meets the published conditions. Slower than a mini-competition, and used when no framework covers the need.
The formal check that a system, its people and its written procedures are all ready for it to go live. Any one of the three can stop it.
Normal daily running of a live system by the department that owns it, after the project has ended and the team has gone.
The work of getting people and processes ready to work in a new way. It is the largest cause of a technically successful system nobody uses.
The PM2 artefact setting out what the project will buy from outside, from whom, on what terms and how the supplier will be managed.
glossary.more: In the story the Appropriate Governance Body is Accountable for it, which surprises the Project Steering Committee.

glossary.d: A one-word summary of project health: green, amber or red, sometimes green, yellow or red. Useful only if the thresholds were agreed in advance.
The part of the capital that members have actually transferred in cash, about 81 billion euro. It is invested conservatively and is never lent out.
glossary.more: It is the cushion that lets the ESM borrow cheaply. It is not the money that is lent.

glossary.d: A time-limited credit line created in May 2020 for healthcare and prevention costs of the Covid-19 crisis. No country drew on it and it expired at the end of 2022.
Running the old and new systems on the same real work at the same time and comparing the results. The only honest proof that the new system is right.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR runs parallel from 08 Jan to 30 Apr 2028.

glossary.d: The system that formats a payment instruction and sends it on to the banks that will move the money. It is the last system the instruction passes through before cash leaves.
The formatted electronic order sent over a secure banking network telling a bank to move money. If a field is wrong the message is rejected, not corrected.
Precautionary Conditioned Credit Line: standby support for a country whose economy is fundamentally sound and which meets published benchmarks on deficit, debt and imbalances.
A self-reported estimate of how far a task has got. Easy to give, hard to check, and the reason earned value exists.
The standing departments that carry on after a project team is dissolved. Benefits that appear after closure are tracked by them, not by the project.
One person working for one day, written PD. The unit PM2 uses for effort, deliberately separate from how long the work takes in calendar time.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR is 3,100 person-days across 26 months, roughly five to six people full time.

glossary.d: Any information about a person who can be identified from it, directly or indirectly. Names, staff numbers and account details all count.
A checkpoint at which a project must be approved before the next phase may start. PM2 has three: Ready for Planning, Ready for Executing, Ready for Closing.
The formal meeting that opens the Planning Phase for the whole project team, once the Ready for Planning gate has been passed.
glossary.more: Held on 09 Apr 2026 for Project CASTOR.

glossary.d: Loans funded from one shared pot of borrowing rather than each from its own matching bond, so that the funding cost is shared across all borrowers.
Proposed work after the project ends: fixes, extensions, follow-up projects, and the checks that the benefits actually arrived.
Standby ESM support for a country that still has market access, arranged before trouble arrives. It comes in two forms, PCCL and ECCL, and is often never drawn.
Where a security is sold for the first time, by the organisation issuing it, to raise money.
An ESM instrument, written PMSF, under which the ESM buys newly issued bonds directly from a member state so that an auction does not fail.
The borrowed amount itself, as opposed to the interest paid for having it. A repayment is usually a mixture of the two, and the split is accounted for separately.
Setting an instrument up in a system as adjustable settings rather than as new program code, so that a trained business user can add or change one.
glossary.more: Success criterion SC3 depends on it entirely: nine months of coding becomes six weeks of configuration.

glossary.d: A euro area country receiving financial assistance under an agreed reform programme. Five have existed: Ireland, Portugal, Greece, Spain and Cyprus.
The document in which the Project Owner formally accepts the project as finished. PM2 marks it as produced if required.
The document that defines what the project will actually do: scope, deliverables, milestones, cost, risks and roles. It turns an approved Business Case into a project.
The specialists who actually build the deliverables, written PCT, coordinated by the Project Manager. It may include contractor staff.
glossary.more: Nikola Tesla and Ada Lovelace sit here, alongside dev and test leads.

glossary.d: The document that says how this particular project will be run: approach, processes, rules, roles and which plans exist as separate documents.
glossary.more: Baselined with the Work Plan on 26 Jun 2026.

glossary.d: The short document that asks permission to explore a problem and write a Business Case. It starts the Initiating Phase.
glossary.more: Submitted for Project CASTOR on 12 Jan 2026.

glossary.d: The person, written PM, who runs the project day to day: plans it, coordinates it, reports on it and escalates what cannot be solved at project level.
glossary.more: In this study tool, you.

glossary.d: The client of the project, written PO. Accountable for its success and for the benefits it is supposed to deliver, and chairs the Project Steering Committee.
glossary.more: Florence Nightingale, Head of Lending Operations. She owns the outcome, not the software.

glossary.d: An independent reviewer, written PQA, of the project's process and documents. Does not report to the Project Manager, and that is the whole point.
glossary.more: W. Edwards Deming. He reviews the process, not the person.

glossary.d: The list of every project stakeholder with their role, contact details, interest and importance, used to decide who gets told what.
The project's decision and issue-resolution body, written PSC. Chaired by the Project Owner, with the Solution Provider, the Business Manager and the Project Manager.
An optional support structure, written PSO, providing schedules, minutes, versioning, archiving and methodology help to project teams.
glossary.more: Henry Gantt, who invented the bar chart, runs it in the story.

glossary.d: The support roles around a project, written PST: quality assurance, the project support office, document management, data protection and information security.
The Closing Phase document summarising how the project went, what was delivered, and who now owns the benefits and the open recommendations.
The central store where a closed project's documents are kept so they can be found again years later, by people who were not there.
Accepting a deliverable while a short, listed set of small problems stays open, each with an owner and a date. Also called partial acceptance.
glossary.more: How the reconciliation report dispute is finally resolved in the story.

glossary.d: A decision threshold of 80% of the votes cast, used for ESM decisions that do not require unanimity. Votes are weighted by each country's share of the capital.
Checking that the agreed process is actually being followed. It looks at how the work is done.
Checking that the thing produced is actually good enough. It looks at the output, not the process.
The scored question set a reviewer works through. It is the main input to the Quality Review Report.
A table naming who is Responsible, Accountable, Supporting, Consulted and Informed for each artefact or activity. Exactly one person is Accountable.
glossary.more: Also called a Responsibility Assignment Matrix. Pronounced rasky.

glossary.d: Formal approval of a treaty or treaty change by every state that signed it, each under its own national rules. Until the last one ratifies, nothing takes effect.
glossary.more: The 2021 ESM Treaty reform is still waiting for Italy.

glossary.d: The third PM2 gate, written RfC, between the Executing Phase and the Closing Phase.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR passed it on 22 Jun 2028.

glossary.d: The second PM2 gate, written RfE, between the Planning Phase and the Executing Phase.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR passed it on 03 Jul 2026.

glossary.d: The first PM2 gate, written RfP, between the Initiating Phase and the Planning Phase.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR passed it on 27 Mar 2026.

glossary.d: Checking that the records of two or more systems match, and explaining every difference. After a disbursement, the loan system, the treasury system and the bank statement must all agree.
glossary.more: Success criterion SC2 cuts this from three working days to the same day.

glossary.d: A difference between two records that nobody has explained yet. Every break must be investigated and cleared, never written off because it is small.
The data protection register naming every use of personal data an organisation makes, why, on what legal basis, and for how long.
A fixed set of tests re-run after every change to prove that nothing which used to work has broken.
glossary.more: Shrinking it under time pressure is the most reliable way known to cause a live incident.

glossary.d: Figures an institution must send to supervisors and auditors on a fixed timetable, in a fixed format. The deadlines are not negotiable.
A defined package of working software delivered into use at one time. Splitting a project into releases lets value arrive before the end.
glossary.more: Release 1 on 26 Mar 2027 is the configuration engine; Release 2 on 17 Dec 2027 is straight-through disbursement.

glossary.d: The fixed plan of when interest and principal fall due across a loan's life. The lending system generates it from the loan terms.
The fixed stretch of time a report covers. Stating it removes the commonest ambiguity in status reporting.
The twelve months an institution measures and publishes its performance over. Benefits that need a full year of live running cannot be reported before one has passed.
glossary.more: CASTOR's benefits first become measurable in the 2029 reporting year.

glossary.d: The detailed list of what the system must do, kept as its own document rather than inside the Project Charter.
The document saying how requirements will be gathered, prioritised, approved, changed and traced through to delivery.
A table linking each requirement to the deliverable that implements it and the test that proves it. It is how you show nothing was quietly dropped.
Changing a loan's repayment dates, usually by extending maturities, as a form of relief for the borrower. Every future cash flow has to be recalculated.
The controlled process of dealing with a failing bank so that its critical services continue and taxpayers do not pay, instead of letting it go bankrupt.
A type of person rather than a named one, used to estimate and price work before anybody has been hired or assigned.
Part of a contract price held back by the client until the supplier has fixed the agreed defects. It is the only leverage that survives delivery.
The same money held back, named as a clause in the supplier's contract and released only at final acceptance.
glossary.more: Three similar words: retention, retention (contract), retention period. Only the last one is about documents.

glossary.d: How long a document or record may be kept before it must be archived or deleted. Keeping data longer than needed is itself a breach.
glossary.more: Not the same as retention in a contract, which is money held back.

glossary.d: The amount of risk the stakeholders agree in advance that they are willing to accept. Agreeing it afterwards is not risk appetite, it is hindsight.
In PM2, likelihood multiplied by impact, each scored from 1 to 5, giving a number from 1 to 25. Written RL = L x I.
The register of identified risks with owner, likelihood, impact, risk level and planned response. A risk that is not written down is not managed.
The chosen way of handling a risk: avoid it, transfer it to somebody else, reduce it, or accept it knowingly.
Returning to the old system if the switch-over fails. A rollback plan is only real if it names a decision point, a decider and a last possible moment.
Repaying debt that is falling due by issuing new debt, usually on the same day, so that the funding continues without interruption.
Where securities are traded between investors after they have been issued. The issuer receives nothing from these trades.
An ESM instrument, written SMSF, under which the ESM buys a member state's existing bonds from other investors, to support liquidity when a disorderly market is itself the threat.
Lending an employee to another organisation for a period while their employment contract stays where it was.
glossary.more: Nikola Tesla is seconded from Levallois Systems into the Project Core Team.

glossary.d: The rule that no single person may both start and release the same transaction. Different people must hold the different steps.
A charge that recovers the ESM's operating costs on a loan. It has an upfront component of 50 basis points and a small annual component.
The part of a contract fixing measurable service levels, such as availability or response time, and what happens when they are missed.
The moment a transfer becomes final: the payer's obligation is discharged and the receiver has the money.
The danger that one side of a transaction delivers and the other does not, in the gap between agreeing a deal and settling it.
The authority, written SRB, that decides how a failing bank in the Banking Union is resolved and manages the Single Resolution Fund.
The pot that pays for resolving failing banks in the Banking Union, written SRF. It holds about 80 billion euro, paid in by banks, and reached its target level at the end of 2023.
In PM2, a score of how big an issue or change is, judged by its effect on the project's objectives. It drives who is allowed to decide it.
glossary.more: Do not confuse it with priority, which is about urgency, or with effort, which is about cost.

glossary.d: The manager, written SP, whose unit produces the project's deliverables and who answers for them.
glossary.more: Leonardo da Vinci, Head of IT and Digital, who must be pulled back to the delivery date.

glossary.d: A national government considered as a borrower. Sovereign debt is debt issued by a state.
A short fixed working period, usually two weeks, ending in something that can be demonstrated rather than described.
A list of yes or no checks proving the stakeholder work was actually done, phase by phase, rather than merely intended.
The document attached to a contract describing exactly what the supplier will deliver, to what standard and by when.
Data passing automatically from one system to the next, with nobody retyping it. People still decide and still approve. They just do not re-key.
glossary.more: Usually written STP. It is the core promise of Project CASTOR.

glossary.d: A measurable target from the Business Case that decides whether the project delivered its benefit. It needs a baseline, a target and a unit.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR has five, SC1 to SC5, and none can be fully measured before 2029.

glossary.d: A short table of Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats, used in a Business Case to compare each option on the same four axes.
Adjusting the method to the project: deciding which plans are separate documents, which are short sections, and which are not needed at all.
A separate copy of the system where work can be tried out without touching live money or live data.
The record of who worked how many days on which task. On a time-and-materials contract it is also what the supplier is paid against.
How far a measure may drift from its target before somebody has to act or escalate. Agreed in advance so that nobody has to judge it under pressure.
Everything an option costs across its whole life, written TCO: build or licence, hosting, support, training and eventual decommissioning.
glossary.more: Comparing options on purchase price alone is the classic Business Case mistake.

glossary.d: One instalment of an agreed loan. A large facility is drawn in tranches, and each one is released only when its own conditions have been met.
The plan for moving from the old way of working to the new one: cutover steps, data, handover to operations and the rollback route.
glossary.more: Who owns retraining 40 loan administrators is the fight this artefact exists to settle.

glossary.d: The function that manages an institution's cash, funding and liquidity: it raises the money, holds it and makes sure it is where it needs to be.
How the work will be done: in-house, outsourced, a mix of both, or not yet decided. PM2 asks the question early because it changes the whole plan.
glossary.more: Project CASTOR is a Mix: in-house core team plus outsourced platform implementation.

glossary.d: Testing done by the people who will actually use the system every day, written UAT. They test whether it works for the job, not whether it matches the specification.
The person, written UR, who speaks for the staff who will use the system every day, and who accepts deliverables on their behalf.
glossary.more: Marie Curie, who will not accept a measurement she has not verified herself.

glossary.d: The day the money must actually be sitting in the receiving account and be usable. It is not the day the instruction was sent, nor the day it was booked.
The time of day after which a payment instruction can no longer reach the value date it was meant for. Miss it and the money arrives a day late.
glossary.more: The reason success criterion SC1 measures cycle time in working days.

glossary.d: The gap between what was planned and what actually happened, in time, cost or scope. It is reported, not hidden.
The tree, written WBS, that splits a project into deliverables, work packages, activities and tasks, until each piece is small enough to estimate.
A block of project work small enough to estimate, schedule and give to a single owner.
The combined plan of what will be done, by whom, when and for how much: the work breakdown, the effort estimates and the schedule.
The return an investor actually earns on a bond, given what they paid for it. It moves in the opposite direction to the bond's price.
